speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That on Saturday, May 19th instant, and every Saturday thereafter until the end of the present session, the house shall meet at 3 o'clock in the afternoon, and the order of business and procedure shall be the same as on Fridays.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
In view of the fact that Thursday the 17th and Thursday the 24th instant are holidays, this is a most inconvenient motion to many hon. members. There are many pressing reasons why some hon. members, especially those who sit on this side of the house, will be absent on Thursday and Friday, and to come back on Saturday is a highly inconvenient procedure to everybody who has to be absent from this city.
In addition to that the motion is objectionable inasmuch as it provides that the procedure shall be the same as on Fridays and Friday is one of the days when the Speaker leaves the chair without motion for supply. That the procedure should be the same as on Mondays would not, I think, be an unfair suggestion, because the rule permitting the Speaker on two days to leave the chair without motion for the house to go into supply is only a recent innovation, as a matter of fact dating back to 1913. Prior to that a motion was required whenever the Speaker left the chair for the house to go into supply. If the procedure on Saturdays is made the same as on Fridays, when there is practically nothing but estimates left to deal with, this house will have but one day on which to present its grievances and there are many grievances which the house has to present between now and the end of June. I suggest to the Prime Minister that with the motion as it now stands it is very inconvenient for many members to sit on these two Saturdays, whatever may be done on succeeding Saturdays.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the house be sitting on succeeding Saturdays?

" Mondays I hope that suggestion will meet with the approval of the government; but if not, we can do nothing more than present our position and if necessary move that the word " Mondays " be substituted for the word "Fridays".

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Towards the end of every session for years past the house has met on Saturdays and the order of business on the Saturday has always been similar to that on the Friday. I might mention this further feature which may have escaped the attention of my hon. friend, namely, that on Friday the order provides for the first hour in the evening being devoted to private bills. The government felt in that particular it would perhaps be furthering the wishes of a large number of members if we followed the same procedure as on Fridays.
Make it Tuesday then.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the question is only one of moving an amendment on going into supply my hon. friend will find that he will have plenty of opportunities. There will be the following Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. If such a really serious situation were to develop that an amendment on going into supply on some subsequent Saturday were desirable I have no doubt he will wish to have the house continue in session, for a day or two longer, in which event he will have an opportunity of moving his amendment the following Monday. The government has sought to ascertain, through the whips and in other ways, the general wish of the members; the motion has now been discussed two or three times, and so far as I am able to learn it is as nearly in accordance with the general wish of hon. members as any motion is ever likely to be. In the circumstances I would ask my hon. friend to allow the motion to pass.

Whilst I agree with the motion of the Prime Minister as to taking Saturday afternoons for the business of the government, I must at the same time express my understanding of and sympathy with the attitude taken by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) as to the matter of going into supply. I think it is only right, if Saturdays are to be taken, that every opportunity should be given for presenting whatever grievances hon. members of this house may have.
The complaint;, however, of the hon. leader of the opposition, that the taking of Saturdays is objectionable on the ground that hon. members want to leave the house on Friday or Wednesday night and be away until the

following Monday is not an argument that is very potent with those of us who have to stay here from the beginning till the very conclusion of the session. Although I have a very deep sympathy with hon. members whose business or social engagements entice them away from the happy surroundings of this house for several days at the end of the week, I do not feel that public business should be held up on that account. But I do think that the Prime Minister should give to the hon. leader of the opposition the opportunity of allowing supply to be moved in the ordinary way on Saturday, if Saturdays are to be taken from this on.

I spoke to the minister the other day in regard to this provision, pointing out that in my opinion the intention of the committee had not been borne out. Let us take the case of a man living in British Columbia who applies for a pension which is refused: the intention was that the file should show all the reasons on which the decision was based and on which he might wish to establish his appeal.

Section 4 as it stands in
the present act is in accordance with the suggestions made by the Canadian Legion, and I believe it carries out the suggestions of the committee, based upon the recommendations of the legion. Those suggestions have been incorporated practically verbatim in this section 4.

I do not wish to
create any difference of opinion, but it will be remembered that during the discussion of this question in the committee, while the point of view of the legion was undoubtedly as indicated, there was something else implied. There was evidently a desire that the reasons, or the evidence upon which the decision was based, should be fully set forth. I have been speaking to a representative of the legion since and he said, "We should like to go that far, but we don't know whether it will be granted". I think it is only fair that this should be done. For example, a man applies for a pension and the information comes back, "Your application has been considered by the board and it has been decided that the bronchitis in your case is pre-enlistment". To enable this man to go on to an appeal, it is desirable to know upon what evidence it has been decided that the bronchitis is pre-enlistment so that the appellant may be in a position to furnish counter evidence. That is only fair. And it is only for purposes of appeal. If we included in this section a stipulation that there should be disclosed such evidence as is required for these purposes, the reasons would have to be given for the decision that the disability was either pre-enlistment or post discharge. Only upon that evidence can the man make his appeal.

The section as drafted
is word for word the recommendation of the committee.
We agree.
But the discussion went further.

On the file there would
appear all the evidence submitted. I do not
think you could expect, in the judgment of the board, which is inserted in a form, that there should be a complete consideration of all the certificates pro and con and of all the medical evidence upon which it was found that the disability was either post discharge or pre-enlistment. That is on the file and is available to the soldier's adviser. What the ex-service man really wanted was some provision which would obviate the clash, which apparently has frequently occurred, between the board of pension commissioners and the federal appeal board in connection with the diagnosis. In some cases a man was suffering from a disability which the doctors found it impracticable to actually name; as to the disease which gave rise to the disability there was a difference of opinion between the board of pension commissioners and the federal appeal board, and it was held that the federal appeal board had no jurisdiction. It is this difference of view which the present section is designed to meet. The old section set forth the ground on which pensions were awarded or refused, and that has been amplified into three subsections setting out, first, the medical classification of the injury or disease causing the disability on which the claim is based; secondly, the medical classification of every injury or disease which the board considers in dealing with the application; and, thirdly, an absolute statement as to whether the board found that the injury or disease was either post discharge or pre-enlistment or whether it was an aggravation of a condition resultant from service. I do not think you could give very much more in the way of particulars in a judgment unless you set out the file.

But the information desired is not on the file. Let me give a concrete case. A certain ex-service man applies for a pension on account of asthma and the board decide that the asthma was pre-enlistment. The man has submitted all the evidence he can possibly get to prove that it was not pre-enlistment and there is nothing on the file to show on what ground the board concluded that it was. There should be some evidence in that direction; they might get the evidence from some neighbour or other person to show that the man had suffered from asthma before enlistment. But, as I say, there is nothing on the file to that effect. It is cases of this description to which we refer; you do not get on the file the reasons for the board's conclusion. We want to know just why they have come to a certain conclusion-what evidence there is for their decision.

I am not a medical man; the hon. gentleman has the advantage of me. Generally speaking, however, if there is a decision that the asthma-or whatever the disease may be-was pre-enlistment there would surely be evidence forthcoming, from the family or from someone who knew the man, in regard to the attacks from which he had suffered. That evidence might come from a great many sources and it is all on the file. I will quite agree with my hon. friend; if it is a case where the board deliberately made a finding with no evidence at all, the file itself would show that, but this is only asking them to set out what is not on the file. I do submit that we are getting into the realm of administration and out of the statutory provisions altogether. I have repeatedly urged that the pension board, when they advise a man as to pension being refused, should give him some idea of the ground on which the refusal is made, to let him know what kind of evidence he should adduce in order to support his case. That was one of the reasons why the soldiers' advisers were appointed, in order that they might go over these files and tell the man what sort of evidence he should have.

I believe the committee did not quite know really what they wanted. If you consider these first three subsections, they could be answered by one word, such as bronchitis, tuberculosis, arteriosclerosis or something of that kind.

In order that we might
have something concrete before us I wonder if my hon. friends think their case would be met if, in addition to the three subsections we have already, we re-enacted the old subsection (b), which required that the board of pension commissioners set out the grounds on which pension was awarded or refused.
I think that would help.

The words " two or three years " were substituted for the words " not to exceed five years I understand in the committee there was some doubt as to whether the use of that term " not to exceed five years " would exclude them from further appointment, and they decided to reduce the term to from two to three years. Was that not what was intended by the Ralston report, namely, that it would not be a permanent body, but rather that to clear up the situation they would be a charge on the public service for a limited number of years?
That is true.

But in view of the
amendments that are now being made to the act in the endeavour to meet the situations that experience has taught us should be met by legislation, the necessity for this board will become less and less apparent. That is, in the operation of the act as the committee has now amended it, there should be less necessity for the appeal board to act.
We are now giving the appeal board direct jurisdiction over the meritorious clause, which is the one which will be invoked more and more as the years go by.
That is the minister's personal view?

In consultation
with the Department of Justice we have had the following amendment suggested which would replace the amendment as it came from the committee:
Every member of the board shall hold office during pleasure or such limited period of time not exceeding five years as the governor in council may prescribe, and shall be eligible for re-appointment from time to time as in the case of the first appointment, provided that any member who is appointed for a fixed period of time shall be removable for cause.
It is just a question whether the period of two or three years will attract the men that we should have on a board of that character, or whether we should extend the period to five years.
There seem to have been a good many applicants for the job.

I am unalterably opposed to long appointments, I do not care whether they are on committees or on the bench or anywhere else. When you appoint a man to a position for ten or twenty years, no matter who he is, where he is responsible practically to nobody, he becomes autocratic, domineering and instead of being more efficient, he becomes less efficient. There is nothing like keeping people keyed up to their jobs. I am opposed to extending the time limit. In fact I moved in the committee that the pension board be brought under the same regulations as the appeal board, and I can see no reason why there should be a distinction between them. I am not impressed with the idea that you have to make long-term appointments in order to get good men. If a man 'has the ability, the inclination, the ambition, he will take chances on making good. All he wants is the chance, and you are making a mistake in fixing long-term appointments for these offices. Nearly everyone who is on the committee was impressed, rightly or wrongly, with the fact that there was a lack of harmony between the soldiers and both of these boards. It is no use endeavouring to disguise that fact. The soldiers were complaining not so much about the law and the bulk of the regulations as about the spirit in which the act was being administered. A large part of our work was to correct the act so as to make it absolutely compulsory for both of these boards to do what we wanted them to do. As a matter of fact we were restricting what you might call the liberty of each of these boards and compelling them to carry out the specific desire of parliament.
It is a mistake to increase that tenure of office of this board and the board of pension commissioners could to advantage be put under similar regulations as the appeal board. If you have good men on the board, you have the privilege of reappointing them. If you do not have good men, they automatically fall by the wayside and you do not have to cause ill feeling by dismissing them. In the end if you limit the term of office of these boards you have greater harmony and greater satisfaction expressed by the soldiers. If you are going to make the term ten years with eligibility for reappointment, that means twenty years, which will carry them through the lifetime of a large number of the soldiers. I am positively opposed to long appointments. On one occasion I suggested to the Minister of Justice that he should get the senators to retire at a certain age. In the railway commission I think the ten-year limit is the right

principle to follow. We should place in these positions younger men who will be more energetic, more ambitious and who will probably throw greater enthusiasm and energy into the work.

Seven.

Does the minister think this
section is workable? I understand there are seven members on the board and it reads:

split them up. I took some interest in this and I think the hon. member from Muskoka perhaps misapprehends the section as drafted and the suggestion made by the minister. subsection 2 of section 50. Section 50 says:

I understand that in the committee there arose the question as to whether or not the phrase "not to exceed five years" did not mean the aggregate of all the reappointments which could be made; in other words, that if a man were appointed for two years and then for three years, would npt the power of reappointment be deemed to be exhausted? The other point is this: Under the act, and the suggestion of the committee, there is no limit, as I have pointed out, to the appointment of the chairman or to the appointment of any other member that the first member of the board, and it has been suggested by the minister, and is embodied in the section which he proposes, that everybody shall be limited. It seemed to me that that was advisable.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition referred to the report of the commission with which I happened to be connected. I find here that their recommendation for the period of appointment to the federal appeal board was five years. It seemed to me that was sound. In the first place, it did not provide for life appointment or for a long permanency, but for some permanency so that a man might have the expectation of some reasonable period of employment, and thus be willing to cut himself off from something else and perfect himself in this work. The suggestion made here is that if you appoint a man first for two years, and he is a good man and you want to reappoint him, you cannot reappoint him for more than three years at the very outside.
But you could continue to reappoint him.
Quite right.

I would certainly agree with
that.

And the five years makes it so that the man can feel, "I do not have to depend upon the whim of somebody to reappoint me; I have at least five years service before me, so I will take my chance and go into the service."
There are a great many applicants, unfortunately.

Yes, and perhaps they are not all qualified. It is not everybody who is qualified for the pension board or the appeal board. A man requires not only medical and legal or business experience, but he has to be wise as a serpent and harmless as a dove as well.

Some of them are the
latter.

And therefore it seems
to me that it is worth while to consider giving some permanency to the appointment, providing you have a good man who has served for two or three years-
What are the salaries?

For the chairman, $7,000, and $6,000 for the others. The amendment which the minister suggests does two things. It puts a limit on everybody's appointment -the chairman's and appointments which would be called first appointments; they are not to exceed five years-and secondly it puts a limit on reappointment, which is not to exceed five years. As the leader of the opposition says, in the course of time the federal appeal board may work itself out of a job, but that is not going to be for a long time yet, I am afraid, and the amendments that are passing this year are the reverse of cutting them out of work; they are giving them additional work and additional responsibility, and perhaps imposing qualifications which were not thought of when the board was first appointed.

I do not think the minister just caught my point. It is pretty hard to discuss this matter without being considered personal, but I do not wish to be considered personal in what I say in regard to either the federal appeal board or the pension board. As a matter of fact, I know very few of the members. But the point is this: If the minister goes on the assumption that he has a perfect board now, and wants to keep them all on, he might just as well pass an age limit for their retirement at seventy-five or eighty years, but the impression we got in the committee was not that the board is perfect, but that it is far from being perfect, and the federal appeal board is just as bad as the pension board, or worse. If the minister is going to raise the period-
He is not raising it.

I thought you were
making it five years.
It is five years now. This is cutting it down to two and three years, but it is making it so that you can reappoint a man.

I thought the minister
was proposing an amendment to make it five years.

That is my point. It
should be for two or three years.

the act now.

I am not saying that
in a personal way at all, but I think you would get better satisfaction that way.

Because there is the right to reappoint for five years, you are not obliged to exercise it; discretion may be used under that section. I am strongly inclined to think that if you got a good man, and offered him a reappointment for one or two years, he might not care to accept it. It seems to me that a person would have very carefully to consider accepting a five-year appointment, because after that time, if his services were dispensed with, what would he do? I prefer leaving the law in its present form.
Would my hon. friend have that apply to everybody? In other words, cut out the word "first" in the first line of subsection 4?
Yes.
As it is now there is a question whether the governor in council could not appoint some of them for ten years.
It would work no hardship to put them all on the same basis.
It keeps them "on their toes", as one hon, member put it.

I quite agree.
Mr. (McPHERSON: Under clause 4 in the original act there was power to reappoint "for such further period, not to exceed five years." This amendment says that they "shall be eligible for reappointment for such further terms of two or three years." Would not this [Mr. Ralston.l
be restrictive to one reappointment? I agree with my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) that the advantages of a shorter term were shown before the committee. I rather think the proposed amendment would limit the term either to two or three years. The minister suggests a five-year term. Personally I am not very much interested in whether the term be two, three or five years, provided there is a reasonably short appointment and a short reappointment so these men wil be kept on their toes and give good service to the public by looking after the soldiers properly.

This is the amendment suggested, and I think it will meet my hon. friend's views:
Every member of the board shall hold office during pleasure, or for such limited period of time, not exceeding five years, as the governor in council may prescribe; and shall be eligible for reappointment from time to time in the ease of a first appointment, provided that any member who is appointed for a fixed period of time shall be removable for cause.

A member of the board might be reappointed for a further period, but not longer chan the original term. All the members would be removable for cause.

The words "during
pleasure" would have no value at all.
If you appoint them during pleasure the appointments are probationary.

This was all carefully considered in the special committee, and the amendment in section 29 represents the conclusion arrived at, with the possible exception of the word "first" in the third line. I think if you eliminate that word the subsection represents exactly what the .committee wanted in the way of legislation. Does my hon. friend find in the subsection any power at all for a recurrent reappointment?
Yes. He "shall be eligible for reappointment for such further terms of two or three years."
There are two classes of terms, but surely it does not limit the reappointments.
Is not that just what it does do?
I would not think so. The language may be ambiguous, but it can be clarified.
Is it not to provide for staggered appointments, one for two years and the other for three?
Yes.
Could not the subsection be clarified by making it read, "for one or more periods of two or three years"?
With all respect, I do not think much of the two- or three-year limitation.

I suppose this is to ensure that you will always have some members on the board who had been on previously, the first half being appointed for two years, the other half for three years, and they would be reappointed respectively for three and two years.
Yes.

I do not think that will remove any ambiguity. The suggestion here is to give the governor in council power to appoint up to five years; then they can regulate any man by reappointing him for a shorter or longer period.

But you have your different periods in your original appointments, some for two and some for three years. The future appointments could all be for two or three years. You do not need to step them; you have already done so. Some will drop out in 1940, some in 1941, and so on.
When the appeal board was first formed I think it was expected that it would not continue for more than five years.

M!r. KING (Kootenay): Quite so. But if this bill is accepted the appeal board will be continued for a considerable period, and it seems to me you will find difficulty in getting the type of men you need to accept appointments for such a short term.
You would get as good as you get now. I will give you a hundred of them before six o'clock.
To get the better type of men we have to extend the period to five years; I am not sure it should not be ten.

The period of time should not be longer than five years, having regard to the conditions which first brought this court of appeal into existence. The Minister of National Defence in dealing with the matter originally did not contemplate the possibility of the board being in existence for any length of time. Circumstances have now made it likely that- it will continue for many years. Under those conditions it is essential, as the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson) and the member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) said, that these men should have a continued thought of the importance of their office and not get into a state of mind where they would not be as desirous of discharging their duties as they were when originally appointed. If you appoint them during pleasure, or for a period not exceeding three years, it seems to me you have done justice to the whole situation by imposing on them always the thought that they must discharge their duties properly, because there has been much complaint that the entire personnel of the board is of one political faith. That in itself is wrong. I put it to the minister, if in a board like this a total disregard of political considerations should not prevail. I have been told so frequently by returned men, "They are all of one political faith on that appeal board. What hope is there for me?" That is a wrong state of mind on their part, but it is brought about by a wrong attitude on the part of the government who appoint the appeal board. The appeal board should be appointed without regard to anything of this sort. That is my view at any rate.

I may call the attention of the minister to the fact that the chairman of the appeal board was at one time on the pension board and was removed.

time chief medical adviser, but not a commissioner.

One point I would
emphasize is this: These appointees should be men who served in France and had some experience in the front line. This is coming to them. The amendment
is only proposed; I have not moved it. The committee reported unanimously and the house accepted their recommendation and it is not my purpose to bring about any disagreement between its members. The board said, "We will not allow you to pay for the land the price which you think you ought to pay because you do not know very much about it." As soon as the inspector came back to the office of the board the applicant was informed that the land had been valued at so much, and the soldier was asked to pay one-tenth of the price in cash. If he bought a $4,000 farm he had to put his hand in his pocket and pay over $400 to the board as further security. Then they bought the land, taking the deed in the name of the crown, and the soldier settler having paid his $400 took back an agreement for sale.
After having gone through all that he went on the land, but he could not sell a bushel of grain except with the consent of the soldier settlement board. I have documents on file to the effect that the soldier settlement board had to give their consent before grain could be sold, and they stated how much of the sale price they were to receive. In addition to that they sent out inspectors who watched the settler to satisfy themselves that he was doing right with the land and that their security was still good. If he secured a loan on cattle, those cattle remained in the name of the board; he could not sell a cow and could do nothing with the products of those cattle unless he received the approval of the board. The inspector would come around and say, "Where are those cattle; where is the increase? What have you done with it?" He was restricted in all quarters; he could do nothing except with the consent of the board. The whole purpose of that procedure was to make certain that the land would be valued at a price at which the board could recoup themselves; then they received one-tenth of the amount from the settler, and finally they made sure that the settler could not dispose of anything unless the board were satisfied that they would get their share of the sale price. Nothing was said to the settler about a homestead which he might take up, but after all that procedure the board now propose that when the settler fails and they have to take back that land, as would be done by a mortgage company, they shall put their hands on his homestead as security for the amount still owing.
No.

Who said no? The
amendment states:
When a settler obtains Dominion lands, whether by soldier grant or otherwise, and thereafter secures the approval of the board to any advance to him pursuant to this act, while there is owing by him to the board any sum or sums of money...
If the settler has taken up a homestead, that homestead is encumbered with a charge for the debt he may owe the board. A mortgage company would not proceed in that way, and I do not see why a soldier settlei should have land which was not considered when the original agreement was made encumbered in this way.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is wrong there, if the settler did not have the homestead at the time he secured the advance.

But nothing was said
about it in the agreement; if it had been included then, there could be no objection, if the agreement under which he bought the land from the government included the homestead, there would be no need for this act.

I am not sure that
I quite understand how this amendment will apply. I will just give the minister a specific case. Here is a soldier who recently lost not only the land he had purchased from the board, but his homestead which was encumbered according to his agreement. The board have foreclosed on the land he secured from them and on his homestead. Under the act recently passed by this house this soldier settler wants to take up a second homestead, and in that case I wonder if that second homestead will be encumbered to secure any indebtedness which might be still charged against him?
I think it is quite clear that any homestead he may take up subsequently will not be charged with any previous debt owing .by him to the board.
It says, "When a settler obtains or has obtained."

I am referring to the
question put by the hon. member for Mackenzie. If he will look at the language of the new section 26 he will find the following:
"When a settler obtains or has obtained Dominion lands, whether by soldier grant or otherwise, such lands shall be subject to a first charge in favour of the board for any sum owing to the board in respect of any sale or advance thereafter approved for and made to him by the board pursuant to this act and no patent shall be issued to such settler for such lands until the amount of such sum so owing with accrued interest has been fully repaid."

Soldier Settlement Act

So if there were a sale made to him before he gets his homestead, or if any advance were made to him before then, his homestead will be free from the charge.

There is one word which I
think should be changed; I refer to the word "sale" in line twelve. This section says that such lands shall be held as security for any sum owing in respect of such sale. It is not in respect of a sale but in respect of a purchase; the debt is owing by the man who bought the land. I did not think any obligation rested upon the man who sold the land; I thought the obligation was on the man who bought the land and did not pay for it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It deals
with the sale to the soldier or the advance made to him.

I think it is

On section 2-Revaluation of land.

I would like to ask the
minister the question which I propounded a moment ago, as to whether or not section 68 could not be further amended by providing that lands which have been purchased with money advanced by the board, for which mortgages have been given, should be subject to revaluation in the same way as other lands mentioned in the section. It seemed to me incredible that such a limitation should exist, having regard to what parliament did last year, yet the Department of Justice has told the department presided over by the Minister of Immigration and Colonization that we could not revalue those lands.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that this matter was very thoroughly discussed in the committee, and perhaps there were good reasons why that is not embodied in this bill.

It is included, if I might say a word in explanation. I think the purport of section 2 is to cover just those cases which the leader of the opposition has in mind. There were two soldier settlement schemes, the one of 1917 and the other of 1919. Under the 1919 scheme title was taken by the board, who sold the land to the soldier under an agreement for sale. Under the 1917 scheme there was no such procedure; the money was advanced to the soldier, who

bought the land, obtained title in his own name and gave a mortgage back to the board. The purpose of this section 2 is that the revaluation scheme shall be applied to those persons who had obtained an advance under the 1917 act, which advance was used in the purchase of agricultural land. I think section 2 carries into effect the very object which the leader of the opposition referred to.

It occurs to me, Mr. Chairman, that the language should be sufficiently comprehensive to cover the point I have raised, as that appears to have been the intention of the committee. I shall treat it as though it were, although I was somewhat surprised when the department ruled that they could not deal with it. Subsection (a) of section 2 will meet the situation with respect to indebtedness to the board, and subsection (b) will meet the situation where the price has been paid, with the approval of the board, for the land and improvements. I do not think it is made abundantly clear that that is what was intended to be done, but we will take it for granted.

It was because of the
ruling of the Justice department that this question came before the special committee.

It is next to impossible for any member to appreciate what this does. I am not saying that there is anything wrong with it, but we have not the act before us. If we had the section of the act we would know what it covers, and then we could see if there was an error made. All I have to say is that if there is any distinction between the soldier who gets an allowance and a revaluation where there is no mortgage, and the one who cannot have a revaluation where there is a mortgage, it would seem to be most inequitable. A mortgage should not control the thing at all. What does control it is the first sale, and if that sale was made at too high a price; if the revaluation shows that he paid $5,000 for lands that were worth only $3,000, he should be allowed the difference; there is no doubt about that.
Only the first sale, with the participation of the board.

I have heard what my leader says regarding what is intended, and I have heard the hon. member say that this implements that intention, but I have not heard anybody quote the act. I do not say that this does not cover it, but surely it could be made clear and we would not have to guess at it. The Minister of the Interior did not seem to have any too much confidence about it, but possibly he was just speaking

Soldier Settlement Act
with that usual caution that characterizes him. Let us have the section read to us, and also the amendments.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I shall be
very glad to do that. My reason for being cautious is that I have found it pays to be cautious when I am talking to a group of lawyers. Section 68 reads as follows: Notwithstanding anything in this act, a settler who has agreed to purchase any land from the board, who has not assigned or transferred his interest in his land-
That is amended in the following manner: (a) by inserting immediately after the word "who' where it first appears in the second line thereof, the following:-

Then (b) amends subsection (c) of section 68. My hon. friend does not want me to read the whole section? I will just read the amended sections.
That will be all right.

speechtext:
I will read down to where the amendment takes place: (c) The depreciation in value to be determined shall be the amount by which, through no neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler, the price at which the board agreed to sell the land and improvements to the settler
Then comes the amendment:
-or the price under the former act paid by the settler with the approval of the board for the land and improvements

-exceeds the present value, and in determining the present value of the land, improvements made by the settler shall not be included.

I made a proposal to the minister the other day that when he brought this act back he include in it a provision to make the employees of this department permanent. The same day the Minister of Health, in his bill to amalgamate the departments of Health and Pensions, brought in a provision which, in effect, makes the employees of that department permanent, and thereby subject to the Civil Service Act and entitled to superannuation. The employees of this department are in exactly the same position. They have been in this department nearly ten years, and they have done and are doing very important work. I understand that they are doing the colonization work for the Immigration department, in addition to administering the Soldier Settlement Act. 56103-189J
I understand also that they are doing colonization work, or a large portion of it, for the railway. Surely under the circumstances these men should be made permanent and should be given the same opportunity and treatment as the other civil servants. The fact that they are, in the main, soldiers in my opinion makes their case that much stronger. I cannot understand why they have been kept out of this right for ten years. I think this offers a very convenient opportunity to make these employees civil servants and entitled to the provisions of the Civil Service Act and superannuation.

I was considering bringing
them under the Civil Service Commission at the next session of the house. However, if there is any strong desire in the house that it should be done this session, it probably could be done. I should prefer, however, to wait until after the report comes from the committee that, is now inquiring into immigration matters.
Is it true that they are doing colonization work for the Immigration department?
Yes.
And it is true that they are doing a large portion of the colonization work for the railway?

The railways do not admit
it.

Is it true they are doing
something?

I think they do.
Mr. CLARK. Then is not their case unanswerable?

I think they have a very
good case.

Is it not a very simple
amendment that is required?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Having had some experience myself, I did not wish to stand in the way of any department of the government coming under the Civil Service Act. That is not my intention, but I think it would be well to wait at least until the report of the committee now dealing with immigration matters is made, because it will have some bearing, undoubtedly, on whether this organization known as the soldier settlement board is to be a permanent one or not. They certainly are not required to be permanent to administer this act alone. They have been doing, as my hon. frend has pointed
Soldier Settlement Act

out, a considerable amount of colonization work; there is no doubt about that. I think the committee which is inquiring into these matters will have something to say as to that, and I suggest that it might be well to leave this matter until the committee has reported.

Mr. Chairman, I hope
the minister will deal with this matter at this session. I have received a very large number of letters and telegrams from gentlemen whom I do not know, residing in various parts of western Canada, asking that the matter be impressed upon the attention of the government at the present session of parliament. Having regard to the service they have rendered and the responsibilities they discharge, and the willingness of the minister, as he has himself stated, favourably to consider the matter, I think that this should be dealt with at the present session. We hope that he will do this without necessitating our endeavouring to move an amendment on the third reading of this measure in view of the representations that have been made from various parts of Canada, if the bill could be dealt with by an added section at the instance of the minister himself, that would be much more pleasing to us than if we were compelled to make a motion which I suppose the government, with its majority, could easily vote down.
I have no serious objection to that. Of course I would have to consult the Prime Minister and the government before introducing an amendment of this kind.
Quite so.

There is just one objection
that might be offered to that suggestion and that is whether it is necessary to have the organization made permanent in character. It is quite fair for the employees to ask to be placed on a permanent basis, but I question whether Canada should contemplate making the soldier settlement board a permanent body in the government service. Surely the work of the settlement board will be completed in a few years and therefore I do not think we should say definitely now that for a long period of years we shall require a number of these men in colonization work. I do not really know whether that is necessary.

My experience is that the
colonization end is the bigest end of the immigration work. As Minister of Immigration my opinion is that their work will be necessary for many years to come.

I should like to ask the
minister in charge when we are going to get
[Mr. C. A. Stewart. 1
some action on this revaluation. I think the question is appropriate as the title of the section is "revaluation of land". Revaluation was long overdue when the act was passed in 1926. The legislation was delayed a year owing to the defeat of the government. It has been passed for more than a year now. All claims had to be entered before October last; that is seven months ago, and as yet I have not heard that any of the settlers in my district have had their claims finally settled. Their claims have been investigated and I think, generally speaking, a number of claims throughout Canada have been satisfactorily arranged so far, but they have not yet the authority of law. These men are kept sort of dangling between the devil and the deep sea, not knowing what they will get or whether they will get anything in the way of revaluation. I should like to know whether any progress has been made. Can the minister give me some definite assurance when the matter is to be, if not wound up, at least proceeded with to the extent of making progress.

Without repeating it, I
should like to associate myself with what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has so well said. The other day there came to my attention a case of considerable hardship. As the hon. member said, the settler is left suspended between the devil and the deep sea. He is perfectly willing to take a swim if the opportunity offers, but he must resist with all his power the effort made to drive him to the gentleman to whom the hon. member has referred, and in terms meaning the government itself.

I can assure the committee
that every endeavour is being made by the land settlement board with extra assistance to have the settlements made as quickly as possible. Many difficulties have arisen but the board is doing its best. My intention was that when my estimates came up I would give a complete report upon the parcels of land examined, the percentage of reductions made, and all other data in connection with the work carried on during the past summer. When my estimates come up I shall be glad to make a statement of that kind.
Have any settlements actually been concluded?
Quite a number.

Supposing the settler
bought school lands, would they be covered by this?

I think so.

Hay Inspection Act

I should like to suggest that the hon. member for East Calgary has certainly left upon those who have not studied the act the impression that this is a new and stringent regulation. As a matter of fact it is a modification of an act which has been in existence since 1919. That is, under the general act all Dominion lands, whether obtained before or after the receipt of a loan, were brought in. Now this is restricted to those he obtained before a loan was made. I may say frankly that I have gone and I shall be prepared to go as far as I consider it possible to go in relieving the soldiers' obligations, but I feel I have some responsibility as a member of parliament to the taxpayers and that is as far as I am prepared to go.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There are two subsections added to section 2, as follows:
(c)	by inspection certificate, to certify the class, quality and/or condition of hay or straw, and such inspection certificates issued by officers appointed by law for that purpose shall be accepted in the courts as prima facie evidence of the particulars therein set out.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The purpose of the two new subsections that have been added is simply to authorize the department to issue certificates of inspection in any case where this method of inspection is invoked. That is not the law now. We are issuing certificates at the present time without any particular authorization, but under this bill we are taking authority to issue the certificates wherever this inspection system is invoked by any hay seller or buyer. It is voluntary legislation, and the principal purpose of the amendment is to reclassify and re-introduce a different system of grades.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have received a letter from some hay growers in Alberta asking whether they would be given some representation on the advisory board when the grades are being established.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Our usual practice, wherever there is an organization of hay producers, or an organization in any other line of business that is being dealt with, is to give representation on the advisory board, and particularly are we desirous of having a representative from each province to represent the hay growers.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I was going to say to the Minister of Justice, to whom I was just speaking, that to make the certificate prima facie evidence in the provincial courts," plus the fact that the legislation is in itself in my judgment an invasion of the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces, will some day invite a declaration from some court that the whole matter is ultra vires of this parliament. I content my self with making that observation, because in your desire to impose the certificates in the provinces by federal legislation, you are now going the whole limit and saying that the courts are bound to take the certificates of this department as prima facie evidence of what the inspectors say regarding the quality of the hay or straw.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT

What is the meaning of the words "applicable to hay grown in the province into which hay is imported"? Dawn in the maritimes, for instance, in Nova Scotia, we have marsh hay, having peculiarities differing substantially from upland hay, although it is tame hay. In New Brunswick and in Prince Edward Island we have the regular order of hay. In Quebec it is largely timothy. In the prairies the hay has distinctive characteristics, and in Alberta it is largely alfalfa. The idea is to work out a system of grades that will take care of the peculiar characteristics of hay that we have throughout Canada.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had the privilege of being present at the sittings of the committee on agriculture

which, some time ago, recommended the adoption of this bill. To-day, I wish to set forth the viewpoint of the province of Quebec, because in this country there are various qualities of hay. I wonder whether Alberta, among other provinces, grows really hay for commercial purposes. I rather think that this bill is especially introduced to please the farmers of Alberta, because there is a variety of other things in their hay. They made the sale of this hay legal, although they admitted that it contained wood and bones of animal carcases, etc.
As I stated, before the committee of agriculture, there are to-day all kinds of new machinery to take care of the hay crop, work which we old timers of Quebec used to do by hand. I am still in favour of grading the hay in the field after it has been mowed and raked separately; we do not gather it in hay-cocks to-day because we have hay loaders. Unfortunately, this makes the hay more difficult to grade. It is different with grain, which we can pass through the fanning-mill, and if necessary we pass it through two or three times so as to obtain grain suitable for seeding. The hay cannot be put through the same process. For instance, in one mording about 20 arpents of hay is cut on a piece of land measuring 15 arpents in length by li to 2 arpents in width; let us suppose that we have in succession a strip of pure clover, another of mixed clover, and a third of fine timothy; in my father's time all the timothy, the pure clover and the mixed clover were handled separately and also placed in different bays in our barns so that we had some fine, medium and ordinary hay. We therefore had a bay of fine hay, a bay of medium hay and a bay of ordinary hay. When it was taken into the bam we could separate the various qualities and we sold the hay according to its grading, Nos. 1, 2 or 3; who could grade the hay to-day while it is being pressed since it is all mixed? Grading is simply impossible. I have been a hay dealer for the last 36 years. I employ, to grade the hay, men with experience, as well qualified as any inspector of the Department of Agriculture. When I purchase 100 tons of hay from a farmer I send an expert; the latter examines two cars and grades them. He places in one car the best quality of hay and that of medium quality in one of the warehouses which we have here and there throughout the district where the hay is bought. If the hay was graded in the fields we could caution the farmer; and he would bring us

Dumping Duty-Mr. Anderson (Halton)
hay of good quality only and we would not be bothered with the kind of hay which we are apt to have in storage. In my own county the farmers bring me good hay, because I tell them to grade and separate it in the fields. I am aware that for a farmer who has very little hay to sell and but one barn, it is harder. However, when farmers have three or four barns at their disposal for hay, they can grade it better than inspectors and dealers. We, the dealers, together with our experts, grade it the best we can, yet the hay is mixed, it can be camouflaged but this does not often happen in a county where the dealer can warn the farmers and tell them to do the right thing. You know that the careful person is always in demand; he goes to the trouble of grading his hay and sells a better product. As a rule we pay him sufficiently to indemnify him for his trouble.
In regard to this measure and many others introduced by the Department of Agriculture, we find it is overdone and it is very annoying to have so many acts in regard to every thing and which have no meaning.
As to the province of Quebec which grows a great deal of both timothy and other hay of good quality, I think that the expert, who championed the bill before the committee of Agriculture (Mr. Clarke), should allow the old dealers to carry on without troubling them. We can assure him that the experts of the Department of Agriculture cannot do any better than we can.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to move an amendment to the motion to go into supply, similar to the amendment that was moved last Tuesday by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie). The subject matter of his amendment was not then pronounced upon by the house, the debate being concluded under the eleven o'clock rule while I was speaking, and consequently I adjourned the debate.
The amendment is being moved again for the purpose of once more bringing to the
attention of the government and the country a matter of considerable importance owing to imports of agricultural products at certain seasons of the year to such an extent as to be injurious to the producers of similar products in the Dominion. These importations affect particularly the farming classes in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia, Quebec and Nova Scotia, and relate to fruits and vegetables and poultry products It will be generally agreed that these may be described as necessaries of life, and are essential to the health of our people, particularly fruit and vegetables when they first come on the market. The sale of the home grown product is injuriously affected by the importation of similar products produced in the United States under conditions that make it impossible for our producers to sell their products at a comparable price. As I have said, fruits are essential to the health of our people, particularly in the summer time; but there are certain seasons of the year when fruits are still more essential to the health of the people of the United States. At those seasons the producers in the United States have a surplus for export, and they dump that surplus into Canada, where it is sold practically to cover the cost of transportation.
Last Tuesday I was interrupted by the adjournment of the house before I could complete my remarks regarding the extent and importance of this industry to Canada and point out the necessity of preserving our home market for Canadian producers. No one will contradict the statement that the home market is the best market for the producers of these particular products. Members of the delegation that interviewed the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a short time ago claimed-and they ought to know what they were talking about

that Canadian-grown fruit and vegetables are the cheapest that the Canadian consumer can buy. All the delegates asked for was that they might be protected against abnormal competition in their home market, and undoubtedly when the surplus fruit and vegetable products of another country are being dumped here the competition is abnormal. The same thing applies to poultry and particularly to eggs, and if the producers of these commodities in Canada are capable of supplying adequately the demands of the Canadian people they should be protected from the imports of the surplus of similar products of other countries.
The delegation which waited upon the government two or three weeks ago was a large body representative of these two particular industries; they came from every

Dumping Duty-Mr. Anderson (Halton)
part of Canada, from the Pacific to the Atlantic. They were here and they presented their case in a very forcible and impressive manner. They stated on that occasion that they would be perfectly willing to accept a seasonal tariff which would enable them to have their own market at that season of the year when their products were available for the home consumer. That surely was a very reasonable request and one which the government could scarcely deny. If they had been asking for a high tariff the year round, to keep out similar products from other countries when they could not be supplied at home, the case would have been different. The Prime Minister, in his speech a week ago, made this observation, as reported at page 2813 of Hansard:
The members of that delegation, for the most part, came here under the impression that the power just referred to had been taken away from the administration.
I quote the Prime Minister in this regard merely to assure him that the delegation had no misunderstanding as regards what they were asking fur. They knew perfectly well that the power had not been taken away from the administration to afford them assistance in connection with the dumping duty; they knew that the dumping clause in the Customs Act had not been repealed. But they did know that the order in cofuncil authorizing the Minister of National Revenue to fix the fair market price of articles coming into Canada had been rescinded. There was no misunderstanding on that point.
The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) opposed the dumping clause on the ground-and he quoted figures-that the application of the clause increased prices in Canada. Mr. Speaker, two mistaken impressions have gone abroad throughout the country in regard to what has been done in connection with these dumping duties. The first is that the government by order in council has deprived the farmer of what little protection the tariff affords him. That is a mistake. The duty as fixed by the parliament of Canada on natural products has not been tampered with. The duty on fruits and vegetables is as it was. The duty on fresh vegetables to-day is 30 per cent and the duty on fresh fruits is specific, being so much a pound or a box or a barrel, as the case may be. With those duties the government have not interfered and so far as I am aware they have no intention of interfering. The other wrong impression that has gone abroad is that the government, by order in council has repealed the dumping clause in so far as it applies to natural products. That also is a mistake. The dumping clause has not been tampered with in the least. The dumping clause requires no order in council for its enforcement. It applies to-day to fruits and vegetables just as much as ever it did. It applies to fruits and vegetables just as much as it does to manufactured articles. What then has happened? Perhaps I can best explain the matter by referring to the statutes themselves. Let me turn to the dumping clause, which is section 6 of chapter 44 of the revised statutes. It reads:
In the ease of articles exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value of the same article when sold for home consumption in the usual and ordinary course in the country whence exported to Canada at the time of its exportation to Canada, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such article, on its importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the article for

export and the said fair market value thereof for home consumption; and such special or dumping duty shall be levied, collected and paid on such article, although it is not otherwise dutiable:
Provided that the said special duty shall not exceed fifteen per cent ad valorem in any case;
And so on, with some further exceptions.
To what does that dumping clause apply? It applies to natural products and manufactured goods alike so long as similar goods are produced in Canada. When does it apply? It applies when those products are being dumped into this country. The definition of dumping as given in the clause is that goods are being dumped when they are being sold for export to Canada at a lower price than that at which they are being sold for consumption in the country of origin. What is the penalty attached? The penalty provided in the dumping clause is a special duty equal to fifteen per cent of the value of the goods. What is the method of enforcement? It requires no order in council, no order from the minister, no order from any official in Ottawa. Any person who is interested can go to the collector of customs at the port of entry and say: "These goods are being dumped into this country; they are being sold to us at a lower price than that at which they are being sold, for home consumption in the country from which they came; here is the proof of my statement." That is all that is required to bring the dumping duty into effect and to have the special duty of 15 per cent added.
Let me turn now to what was section 47a or, as it is now numbered, section 43 of the Customs Act. It reads:
If at any time it appears to the satisfaction of the governor in council on a report from the minister, that natural products of a class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada, either on sale or on consignment, under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously to affect the interests of Canadian producers, the governor in council may, in any case or class of eases, authorize the minister to value such goods for duty, notwithstanding any other provisions of this act, and the value so determined shall be held to be the fair market value thereof.
To what does this apply? It applies only to natural products. When does it apply? So badly did they suffer from conditions that in 1920, after the shipping season of that year, their representations found the ear of the Union government, and in 1921 the valuation clause was placed in the Customs Act, enabling the minister to declare what the value for duty was, on a basis of comparison with the actual cost of production of similar goods imported into this country at a like date. With regard to the second point, I maintain that it is wrong in fact. There are reasons why in my opinion the producer of perishable products should receive perhaps greater attention than the producer of products which are not perishable. The latter does not need to market his products immediately they are ready; the wise business man, with his finger on the pulse of the market, is able to realize when something is backing up, and perhaps he can move his operatives or change his machines to some other article for the time being. In my orchard I prune my trees, irrigate them, cultivate them, spray them, thin the fruit and plant crops between the trees to plough in and enrich the soil, but I have no control over the blossoms. A bountiful crop comes along and naturally I am pleased, although with it my expenses in thinning, hauling and packing go up.
