I hold in my hand a publication issued by the Department of Agriculture called the Egg and Poultry Market Review. Under date of April 3, which was about a day or two after these orders in council were taken off, I read as follows:
Car lots of eggs have been offered in the west at-extras, 31 cents; first, 29 cents; seconds, 26 cents per dozen, f.o.b., freight charges extra.
You see, Mr. Speaker, while the minister had power to put on 45 cents as the fair market price, British Columbia was offering eggs with the dumping duty on as low as 29 cents

Dumping Duty-Mr. Neill
for firsts, which would be the average grade. Does anyone think 29 cents per dozen, ex-Vancouver, is too big a price to pay for that class of eggs? Surely the price has not been unduly increased by this dumping clause. Then again, did the removal of the dumping clause do harm? I will quote the next sentence in this same government report:
Sales have been made on the basis quoted above, but large numbers of these have been cancelled following the notice of the removal of the dumping duty on eggs.
This is a government publication which says, and says truly I have no doubt, that those sales at a fairly low basis were cancelled as soon as it was known that the dumping clause had been removed. In a later issue of the same paper I find:
In large measure the removal of the dumping duty is responsible for the present easiness.
I would call it "uneasiness" so far as the poultrymen are concerned. So we have the evidence out of the government's own paper that the price was not unduly raised, and that it fell away as soon as the dumping duty was taken off.
I have before me the Vancouver Province, a well-known paper, giving the market prices. The price to the farmer for his eggs ran from 24 cents down to 18 cents a dozen, or an average of 21 cents. Would anyone of us like to raise eggs at 21 cents a dozen at the prices for feed that I will now quote from the same paper? No. 2 wheat sells for $2.50 a hundred pounds. May I inform my friends from the prairies that No. 2 wheat in British Columbia does not mean No. 2 Northern. It means No. 6, or sometimes a grade lower than that, a mixture, and sometimes, if the feed merchants feel good-hearted, No. 0 with a mixture of No. 5. We pay $2.50 for that in Vancouver. The price is also quoted for a hundred pounds of oats- $2.70. Some of our older men may go back in memory to the days in Ontario when they could buy eggs for 15, or perhaps as low as 10 cents a dozen; but the farmers did not pay $2.70 for a sack of oats to feed their hens. You never can raise those eggs at 20 cents a dozen. I should like to quote two reputable men. I do not propose to give their names, but I know them well. One has got something like five thousand birds. He writes me:
Last month-
That is March.
Last month I shipped over 10,000 eggs, and I only received over the cost of the month's feed bill $14.20, for a month's work every day, including Sundays, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Fourteen dollars and twenty cents a month. Who would not go poultry farming? He goes on to say:
Something will have to be done soon or B.C. will be shipping eggs from the United States for home consumption.
What the other man says is even worse:
My last shipment of eggs netted me here just 16.59 cents a dozen.
About 16J cents a dozen. He continues:
That is the average. I continually see at wharves and stations on Vancouver island thousands of fine-looking birds being shipped into Vancouver markets, birds in the pink of egg-laying condition being sacrificed after a winter of high-priced feeding. This can only mean that hundreds of poultrymen all over the country are going into the cities again in search of work. Is it not pitiful?
He adds:
There is a great movement to bring more people into the country, for the benefit of the Canadian Pacific and railway companies I suppose, and dump them on the land. What for, for heaven's sake? I am strongly tempted to write the European publications warning them against this step. I feel it as a kind of duty.
I do not know but what he is right. I should like the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) to listen to that. There is a popular feeling that if you throw a man out of the land, success and prosperity is bound to be his.
The argument is sometimes raised, and possibly will be to-day, that we must consider the question of cheap food for the workingman. I have always found the workingman to be no fool. He is strongly against sweated labour; that is, goods produced by labour sweated to the extent that it is very poorly paid. I am quite sure his sympathy will go out to the poultryman who worked a whole month for $14.20. His labour is sweated to the extent that payment for it disappears entirely. No Canadian workingman would stand for a proposition like that. Moreover, our workingmen are quite smart enough to know the inevitable result-the elimination of half the poultry growers, followed by increased prices for eggs and poultry imported from the States.
Another point I made in my resolution was that this action was uncalled for. I certainly would ask this question: Who wanted this action taken? Where did those people come from and when did they ask for it? I do not think the government could possibly answer the question. There was no agitation, no feeling of ill-will, no feeling that anybody was paying too much for eggs. The removal of the dumping duty came as a bolt from the blue, and was thrown in, so to speak, to
Dumping Duly-Mr. Neill

remedy some possible injustice in connection with these other natural products; but it does not apply to the question of eggs, and I protest eggs being included in this matter.
I am not here to discuss the question of tariff. I am not in favour of a high tariff. Some time ago a body of economists, more or less under the aegis of the League of Nations, went on record that it would probably be better for the world at large if a system of free trade were adopted. Yes', the League of Nations is strongly in favour of disarmament, but I never heard them say that only one nation should disarm and the rest should be armed to the teeth. I do not think those economists would ever have seriously put forward the thought that one nation should be the goat of this' idea of free trade- and not only one nation, not only one industry in that nation, but one part of the industry in that nation. That was never contemplated by those men. So long as we have a tariff-and it cannot be denied that we have, with every prospect of keeping it for many years to come-then the farmer and egg producer is as much entitled to his share of that tariff as the manufacturer. And we are not asking for very much, not for the 25, 30 or 35 per cent that the manufacturer gets; we are only asking for what at most comes to 20 per cent, and that only under occasional circumstances.
Adequate protection.

No, I will not split hairs. In desperation we have turned to the market in New Zealand and have sent a shipment there. But what do we run up against in New Zealand? A 20 per cent ad valorem duty. And what have we in return to protect us?
There has always been a dumping duty under every government, Conservative and Liberal alike, but section 6, the dumping clause, is powerless alone. The Conservative government, recognising that fact, passed an extra measure providing for the imposition of an arbitrary dumping duty. The Liberals also recognized it when they took similar action in 1923. We need this extra legislation to give the dumping clause teeth, so to speak.
One word more as to the value of the industry. As I mentioned before the delegation, the egg industry alone-not including poultry -last year in Canada produced something like $80,000,000. This was the revenue from the humble hen. The royal commission on fisheries reported the other day that so great was our fishing industry, so vast its importance, that they would recommend a special department, with a minister at the

head of it, to deal with fisheries alone. And what was the output of our fisheries last year? Only $56,000,000. The egg industry alone, on the other hand, produced last year some $80,000,000. Perhaps we need a ministry of eggs as well. I do not think I am beside the mark when I say that there are probably a quarter of a million of people dependent upon this industry, which is supposedly a side line.
What do we want? We want legislation introduced correcting section 43 and bringing it into line so that section 43 and section 6 may be enforced legally. And we want an assurance that the two will be applied, because nothing else will suffice. If the government gives us that assurance, then this amendment falls to the ground. That is all we want.
I come now to the resolution itself. We are told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that he regards it as a want of confidence motion, and I know it is the custom so to regard such resolutions. But there is nothing in the rules that compels us to treat it as a want of confidence vote. I remember a resolution which we attempted to put through this house some years ago, providing that a government's defeat on a question of this kind should not be held to be a vote of want of confidence, unless followed by a specific resolution to that effect. Had that resolution been adopted, I venture to say that many more hon. members in this house would vote for this amendment than will do so. I submit that this resolution should not necessarily be considered a vote of want of confidence. The very language of the motion indicates that such is not essential. It declares that "in the opinion of the house necessary action should be taken." There is no condemnation of the government for something they have done in the past, which is the usual form of motions of want of confidence. The resolution merely asks that something be done in the future. There are on the order paper probably thirty resolutions which are couched in the same terms, many of which we have discussed. Not one of them would involve the defeat of the government if it carried, for the simple reason that these resolutions are academic. But they would bind the government to some action if they passed. Well, the resolution now before the house is of the same character; it is couched in similar language.
There is one thing which I like about this amendment and which I do not often see in the budget amendments of my hon. friends opposite, and that is its clear-cut and definite nature. Generally speaking, the tariff amend-

Dumping Duty-Mr. Gott
ments of my hon. friends opposite are so vague, so comprehensive and so partisan that it is almost impossible for anyone, trying to look at them from a non-partisan point of view, to make up his mind whether to vote for them or not. In this case it is not so; the resolution is confined to one statement of fact, a definite condition which exists, and it asks that this condition be remedied. It is, as I say, clear-cut, and it is easy to decide on the point. It is easy for every hon. member to say, "I am going to vote for or against a proposition which may mean the preservation in Canada of an industry on which a quarter of a million people are dependent, and of which the output is something like 880,000,000 a year".
I have no quarrel with my hon. friend from Weyburn-with whom, I hope I may say, I am personally friendly-or with any other hon. member if he takes a different view of the matter, provided he is satisfied that he is expressing the views and voting in the interests of his constituents. So far as I am concerned, the interests of my constituents are so plain, the pledge I made them-practically the only pledge I did make-being that I would put their interests first in my consideration, that I cannot do anything else than support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson).
Mr. ECCLES J. GOTT (South Essex): It seems to me that there seems to have been a general disposition, if not an effrontery, on the part of the government to evade the issue that has come before the country through the cancellation of order in council 1088, implemented by authority entrusted to the Minister of National Revenue in section 47a of the Customs Act, now 43. In order to remove any misconception or general misunderstanding as to what had actually been done, I asked the following question of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) on the orders of the day, on April 25, page 2368 of Hansard:
Has the authority given to the Minister of National Revenue to determine the value of fruits and vegetables for the purpose of applying the special or dumping duty been cancelled?
Further I said-I wanted to make the question specific and definite:
By this I do not mean, has order in council 1088 been rescinded, but has section 47a of the Customs Act been so amended as to take away this authority from the minister?
The reply I received from the Minister of National Revenue was:
There has been no amendment to the act whatever. The order in council authorizing the minister to fix values has been cancelled.
I quote from the Border Cities Star, of April 21, the report of a meeting of the Independent Order of Daughters of the Empire held at Hamilton, one of the main consuming centres of Ontario. A despatch dated from Hamilton, April 20, reads:
Yesterday, the final day of the three-day annual meeting of the Provincial Chapter, I.O. D.E., a resolution was passed which will be sent to the federal government asking for a reconsideration of the rescinding of the dumping act in order that the fruit and vegetable grow-ers of Ontario may be protected.
The resolution reads: "Whereas the special dumping act will not be applied during the coming season in the matter of fruits or vegetables: whereas, in consequence our growers will suffer, the Provincial Chapter, I.O.D.E., views with alarm this condition of things and would respectfully urge the government to seriously reconsider this matter, feeling that the Canadian fruit and vegetable growers have every right to protection.
On the order paper I put certain questions appearing as question No. 16, as follows:
1.	Has order in council No. 1088 been rescinded and cancelled?
The answer was, "Yes."
2.	When was same rescinded and cancelled?
Answer: March 19, 1928.
3.	When did the rescission and cancellation become effective?
Answer: March 19, 1928.
4.	Has the tariff board made any recommendation regarding protection for early Canadian fruit and vegetable growers, seasonal or otherwise ?
Answer: The subject is under inqury.
There are hundreds of other questions that have come before the tariff board which are still under inquiry.
5.	If so, what was the substance of such recommendation ?
Answer: Still under inquiry.
6.	Is the government aware that resolutions are being passed by boards of trade, town and city councils, chapters of the Daughters of the Empire and other bodies, protesting against the government's action in rescinding order in council 1088?
Answer: Some resolutions have been received.
Despite this, the Minister of Finance had the precipitance and temerity to tell the delegates who assembled here that this order in council had not been cancelled. This is what he said when speaking to Mr. Fisher, a member of the delegation. Mr. Fisher said:
Now that privilege has been taken away and we feel that we have been discriminated against.
Hon. Mr. Robb: Wait a moment. Who said it was taken away?
Mr. Fisher: Well, maybe I have not used the right word but the order in council making it effective has been withdrawn, as we understand it.
Hon. Mr. Robb: No.
This was said after the Minister of National Revenue, in answer to a question put by my-
Dumping Duty-Mr. Gott

self, stated definitely that it had been cancelled. Now I want to put on record samples of the resolutions which have been received by the government, and first I would refer to one or two which were sent out before the delegation came to Ottawa. The first is dated April 10, and comes from Grimsby:
The fruit growers understand that the order in council authorizing the Minister of National Revenue to fix values for fruits and vegetables under section 43 of the Customs Act, Revised Statutes, has been cancelled. '
Realizing from their experience of the dumping act as administered in former years and as administered in the past two years during (which latter period the minister was authorized to fix values) the apparent impossibility of getting action quickly enough to be of any practical use, they feel that they are virtually being left without the protection of a dumping act unless the power is again given to the minister to fix values.
The very rapid changes which take place in the supplies available and prices in these very perishable lines render it more necessary to have an efficient dumping act in operation to protect this industry than almost any other.
How badly the home market is needed for the industry can be easily verified by application to either loan companies loaning in the fruit areas or banks operating branches in these areas. During the last five or six years there has been a steady shrinkage of the quantities grown in Canada and a big increase in the quantities imported from the United States.
The industry is in vital need of an efficient dumping act and the Ontario growers hope that their members will help to procure for them an anti-dumping clause for their industry which will be effective.
I am going to put one more resolution on record, dated April 17 of this year and coming from the Grimsby chamber of commerce:
Re Cancellation of Special or Dumping Duty
It is with surprise that we learn of the cancellation by order in council of that portion of the dumping act applicable to the fruit and vegetable industries.
Under existing conditions we are satisfied you cannot help but'admit that the fruit and vegetable industries of our Dominion are insufficiently protected to warrant increased production on the part of all agricultural branches of the industry, and the government's recent action is certainly most detrimental. Without the protection which formerly existed all products grown in the United States will have free access to our Canadian markets, whereas the act as previously administered offered a seasonable relief, but with this eliminated you will realize without doubt what will happen to the fruit and vegetable industries.
I direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister to the next part of the resolution :
During the week ending April 11th, 1928, Dominion market reports show importations into Canada of two hundred and eleven cars of fruits and vegetables of a class or kind grown in Canada. These features considered you can readily realize as the season advances,

and our fruits and vegetables grown in Canada by Canadian producers and largely for Canadian consumption, what the result will be under the present existing circumstances. We submit that the Canadian consumer would be materially benefited, if our producers were only
fiven the advantage of the act as formerly in oree, thereby stabilizing conditions to the betterment of all, which fact can be verified by statistics of the past four years.
We solicit your preferred consideration of the above, and trust in your wisdom you will realize the necessity of replacing by order in council the provisions of the act applicable to fruits and vegetables, for without prosperous agricultural conditions we cannot have a prosperous Dominion.
Thanking you in anticipation of your prompt attention and adjustment, thereby maintaining this Canada of ours for the Canadians.
Yours very truly,
Grimsby Chamber of Commerce.
In the report of the proceedings which took place when the delegation was present in Ottawa, I find that the Prime Minister used the following words:
Now that is the only point at issue at the present time that in any way as far as I can see it, is creating a conflict in the minds of some who are interested in this matter.
Under that clause there was passed an order in council. Just how it came to be passed I am not in a position to say. An order in council was passed on the 13th day of July, 1926. That was the first one. That order reads as follows: Whereas the acting Minister of Customs and Excise reports that from information in his possession it is established that fruit and vegetables of a class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada from glutted markets in the United States, at values such as prejudicially or injuriously affect the interests of Canadian producers;
Therefore His Excellency the Governor in Council under and by virtue of the provisions of section 47-A, hereby authorizes the Minister of Customs and Excise to value such fruits and vegetables for duty notwithstanding any other provisions of the Customs Act. the values so determined to be held to be the fair market value thereof.
The Prime Minister said he had no knowledge of where the order in council came from. I would like to have his attention just now, because I took occasion to put this on record once before, and I would like to show him the origin of this order in council. Under date of June 30, 1926, I received the following telegram from the Seacliffe Growers in the riding which I have the honour to represent:
We respectfully wish to draw your attention to the fact growers here have been seriously handicapped by heavy importations of southern cucumbers and tomatoes which have severely hurt marketing of our hothouse crops in this district. We are now about to begin heavy shipments of field crops such as cabbage and tomatoes and if above unfair competition continues serious losses will be sustained by our growers. We would ask you to use every influence to remedy these conditions.

Dumping Duty-Mr. Gott
This telegram was passed over to the Minister of Agriculture, who wrote me saying he had referred the question to the Minister of Finance who in turn referred it to the tariff board, that inactive body which was not, and is not, functioning. On July 2, 1926, I received another wire from the Seacliffe Growers, as follows:
Cabbage crop nearly unsalable. Prices offered would not net growers one cent per pound. Tomatoes in much same position. All owing to import of American stuff which is being dumped in this country at prices that take such low duty that there is no protection to our growers. Cannot something be done to enforce anti-dumping act. This situation has already entailed serious loss to producers in this county.
I would direct attention to the following figures, which probably explain the state of affairs responsible for these telegrams. During the week from June 24 to July 1 inclusive, 1926, there were imported into Canada 128 carloads of tomatoes, which arrived at their ports of entry free from duty, or at least under such low rates of duty as gave no protection to our growers. I would ask the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), who says there were no importations, to try if possible to grasp these figures. In seven days, the cars received at the different points were as follows:
Montreal	 79
Toronto	 35
Winnipeg	  8
Ottawa	 6
Total	 128
During the seven consecutive weeks from May 12 to June 30 of the same year the importation of 1911 carloads of early vegetables threatened destruction to this industry in Canada. Here are the figures for the weeks ending as follows:
May 19	 205
May 26	 230
June 2	 365
June 9	 220
June 16	 260
June 23	 217
June 30	 414
Total	 1,911
I ask the hon. member for Weyburn if there were any importations during that period.
Fortunately for the farmers of Canada, and particularly the farmers of South Essex, whose interests I was trying to protect at the time of this disastrous flood of importations from the United States, a change of government was taking place. The Hon. H. H. Stevens was appointed Acting Minister of Agriculture in the new government. I returned to my
riding and went into the fields of the respective municipalities and ascertained the exact conditions that existed. Under date of July 10, 1926, I wired the Hon. H. H. Stevens as follows:
Vegetable growers of South Essex have drawn my attention forcibly to glutted conditions of their markets making it impossible to dispose of their produce with the result that crops are being left in the field. Government reports issued by the Fruit branch department of Agriculture show hundreds of carloads of competitive vegetables imported weekly-see telegraphic report No. 14 showing 414 cars imported into eleven Canadian centres during the short period of one week. American reports show such crops in the United States being shipped at prices that do not pay cost of transportation to market, far less cost of production, with result that ad valorem duty imposed by our government and based on invoice price at point of production means absolutely no protection against heavy importations. These deplorable conditions existing now with reference to hothouse tomatoes, cabbage, and beans will continue with reference to main crops of field tomatoes and potatoes which are now ready to be harvested, unless some immediate action is taken now by our department. On my return to Essex county I made a personal canvass of the district and find conditions exactly as represented in this wire.
This is the wire that produced order in council No. 1088, for it was passed three days following.
Under the authority of section 47a of the Customs Act and order in council No. 1088, dated July 13th, 1926, the Hon. Acting Minister of Customs and Excise valued certain fruits and vegetable products when imported from the United States, as follows, per pound net:	,
Tomatoes, 5 cents.
I will ask any hon. member opposite if 5 cents a pound is too high a valuation to put on tomatoes.
Cucumbers, 3 cents.
Cabbage, 11 cent.
Celery, 2 cents.
Onions, 11 cents.
Potatoes, 2 cents.
Asparagus, 10 cents.	,
Carrots, 11 cents.	.
Beets, 2 cents.
Lettuce, 3 cents.
Spinach, 3 cents.
Cauliflower, 2J cents.
Peaches, 4 cents.
Raspberries, 17 cents.
It was held that these values should be the fair market value thereof for purposes of application of ad valorem rates of duty and special duty. I have here the bulletin known as appraiser's bulletin No. 3209. The bulletin quotes section 47a of the Customs Act, and explains the application of the special duty,
Dumping Duty-Mr. Gott

or dump duty, and shows its effect in the following conclusion:
At present Mississippi tomatoes in 4-basket crates (15 pounds net) are selling and imported at 60 cents per crate, which is less than the fair market value set above (75 cents per crate). The duty would, therefore, be assessed as follows:-
Regular duty, 30 per cent of 75 cents, 22J cents; special duty, 15 per cent of 75 cents, 111 cents-total 33J cents.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) takes exception to my referring to the warehouse which he built at Leamington as a shed. This was built by the Minister of Agriculture, and I believe he was sincere when he built it. I do not think there is any man in public life who is more sincere with his work than the Minister of Agriculture. When he built this onion warehouse he thought he was doing the onion growers of South Essex a good turn. What the onion growers of South Essex want is the implementing of this order in council which took the duty or tariff on onions from 30 cents to 58 cents. We do not want an onion shed to store our onions in until such time as the American, Spanish and Bermuda onions are on our market, underselling our Canadian farmers. We want the right to have our own market, which is the best market we can have. We want protection and tariff on onions.
I would like to say to the hon. member for Weyburn and to the hon. member for Rose-town (Mr. Evans), who quoted the high prices that were being paid for Canadian products, that after order in council No. 1088 became effective-it took some time to get it effected, but 1 wired from Windsor to the customs department that order in council No. 1088 was not being properly and sufficiently enforced as intended-the importation of surplus produce from the United States ceased almost immediately after it became effective. The producers and consumers in South Essex were both benefited. The producers got more for their products and the consumers paid less, simply because the middleman was eliminated. The consumer also got fresh vegetables every day direct from the farm.
There is not a farmer in South Essex, whether he is Liberal or Conservative, but who is in favour or order in council No. 1088. I sincerely wish that protection in this country was employed in such a way that only the people who vote for it could benefit thereby.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will detain the house only a very few moments. I observed from the debate this afternoon that everyone seems to

be desirous of helping the producer, though there are some who have a different idea of how to go about it. This government has been attacked this afternoon for not protecting the farmer; not doing anything, according to the arguments of the hon. gentleman opposite, to help the farming industry. I also recall that on other occasions this government has been attacked for giving everything to the farmer, and we have been attacked for sacrificing other interests of the country to the farming industry. Hon. gentlemen opposite have attacked us not only in our tariff changes, not only in our reduction of taxes as it applied to farm products and the required farm implements and utensils, but as it applied, in some cases, to the freight rates given to help that industry. Not only in this house, but on the platform during two successive elections, this government has been attacked because of its attitude towards the farming industry. The representatives of the Tory party placarded the billboards of the country advocating-and also in their speeches they advocated-a tariff policy against the United States, a brick for brick policy.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will any person deny that?
The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen denied that in this house dozens of times. It was brick for brick only as applied to agricultural products.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is just what I want, and in a few moments I will show how this brick for brick policy would affect Canadian industry. It has occurred to me that this is but a repetition of the budget debate and the resolution now presented for consideration might very properly have been introduced at the time the budget was introduced. I do not raise this as a point of order; we are not afraid of the vote; we want to know just where the house stands on this particular question. But I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is very questionable whether this resolution is in order, because it is practically and to all intents and purposes the same resolution as was introduced on the budget debate.
I wish just for a moment to deal with the observations of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) who very frankly admitted that he and some of his associates had worked up that flood of telegrams that came to the Prime Minister and all the other ministers for a time. My hon. friend, however, as well as the hon., member for South Essex (Mr. Gott), who has just sat down, apparently misunderstood a statement that I made when the

Dumping Duty-Mr. Robb
delegation waited on the government some time ago. I told that delegation very frankly that the law remained on the statute book just as it stood before. It is true that the order in council enabling one minister of a government, or officials acting for the minister, to fix values was changed, but the law remains as it has been for some years. If hon. gentlemen wish me to take up time in reading it, it is probably just as well to put it on Hansard. This is the law as it stands on the statute book to-day:
If at any time it appears to the satisfaction of the governor in council on a report from the minister, that natural products of a class or kind produced in Canada are being imported into Canada, either on sale or on consignment, under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously to affect the interests of Canadian producers, the governor in council may, in any case or class of cases, authorize the minister to value such goods for duty, notwithstanding any other provisions of this act, and the value so determined shall be held to be the fair market value thereof.
That is section 43 of the Customs Act. The producers of vegetables and fruits in British Columbia, besides the protection contained in the federal law, now enjoy a certain protection through the provincial government, and I should not be surprised if hon. gentlemen at some time, maybe before the end of 1929, will be attacking the provincial government for the very act which that government has in force now, protecting the fruit and vegetable growers of that province.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) regards this not as a want of confidence motion and I imagine he is quite sincere in his view. But looking into the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite I can see that they have no doubt as to what the resolution means. If the amendment carries and the government is defeated on the motion to go into supply in order to vote money to carry on the affairs of the country, my hon. friends opposite will immediately rise and claim that this was a vote of want of confidence in the government, so my hon. friends have no doubt whatever about the matter.
The Prime Minister himself so stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not going to go into any details of figures because some of these have already been given, but I observe that the mover of the resolution as it was presented to the house the other day has no doubt about what they desire. It is not the dumping duty that my hon. friend desires to be imposed; it is an increase in the tariff, because my hon. friend (Mr. Tolmie) stated clearly:
The value of a dumping clause depends, first of all, very greatly upon its continuity and
steady enforcement, so that a man is enabled to figure from one year to another, whether he is a buyer of these products, a dealer, or the producer on the land.

Would that not be clearly shown if we were dead sure of having a dumping clause applied every time that it was necessary? It would be necessarily a fixed tariff if we knew the dumping clause was to be applied when it was necessary. When the Americans were aiming to dump goods into this country it would be ample assurance for the buyers to go ahead and for the producers to produce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend's friends and our friends, the growers of vegetables and fruits, now have an inquiry going on before the tariff board. They have already had three hearings and the hearings are not yet completed. This is a large country and interested parties from all sections have not yet been heard. I am very frank to say that in some cases in this wide country there might be something to be said for a seasonal duty, but
1	propose to show hon. gentlemen opposite who are arguing for a brick for brick policy against the United States, that they are arguing for a policy that in some cases will not increase but reduce the Canadian tariff.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will put this on record and later on I will answer some questions for my hon. friend. What are the Canadian tariffs and the United States tariffs on the items that have been complained of during the debate this evening? The tariffs are as fdllows:
Commodities
Canadian tariff-United States tariff
Apples: 90 cents a barrel; 25 cents a bushel.

Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to take part in this discussion because, I think, that the question introduced in the house by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie), has a very important bearing on our tariff policy. Our most distinguished statesmen have always endeavoured to find a solution to this important problem and quite naturally the question again crops up in the house. As representative of a riding almost exclusively agricultural, especially in that part of the county of Laval-Two Mountains which is known as the garden of Montreal, I wish to request from the government the greatest possible protection, assistance and fairplay on behalf of the farming population of my riding. I further wish to request, and in so dong I am but echoing the eloquent words expressed by the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lancotot)-I wish to request a seasonal tariff for the truck farmers of the county of Laval-Two Mountains and the province of Quebec. Perhaps the government will soon adopt this policy; I hope that such will be the case in the interest of the farming classes.
Let us bear in mind, sir, that the farming class controls the basic industry of this country. Should agriculture fail, our prosperity will dwindle. That is why the motion introduced by the member for Victoria, beam upon one of the most important aspects of our economic life.
I wish to point out to the house, that it is in the interest of all the people in this Dominion, consumers as well as producers, that new markets be found for our natural products which, according to certain specialists on statitsics, could feed 35,000.000 people, while we are barely 9,000,000.
I do not entirely agree with the views of my colleague, the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), when he states that we should equally consider the welfare of all classes of society. Among these classes, which one toils the most? Is it not the farmers who, when dawn is breaking are already on their way to the fields to prepare and put in the seeding? Is it not the farming class which work not 300 days only in the year but 365 days? The farmer has not even his Sundays to himself. The farming class is the one which feeds the people of Canada and the whole world. It is therefore entitled to the greatest possible assistance and fairplay on the part of our governments. That is why I request for the truck farmers of Quebec and the riding of Laval-Two Mountains especially a seasonal

tariff which would abolish the disloyal competition of the United States, our wealthy and powerful neighbours who have climatic
advantages over us.
I have already given my views on this question. When the budget was brought down in the house, the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), introduced a similar motion. I voted against sudh an amendment because I considered that class and sectional interests should give way to considerations making for the general welfare of the country. For the same reason, I shall again support the Liberal government, which offers to the people of this country a sincere and sound administration. I must add that I cannot place my trust in a possible return to power of our hon. friends of the opposition, because in the past they never raised that tariff. I believe that this motion is simply introduced in the house with a political purpose. Having full confidence therefore in the distinguished men who are at present directing the destinies of this country, I shall support the government.

Mr Speaker, I wish to add my protest on behalf of the producers of my district in particular anidl of those of the province of British Columbia in general. I join with my good friend the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) in calling the attention of the government to the result of their action of last month in removing by order in council the powers of the Minister of National Revenue to fix the fair market value of fruit and vegetables, eggs and poultry. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), referring to the representatives of British Columbia, said that they protested against the action of the government in bringing in the Australian treaty so far as eggs were concerned. I do not think that any great protest was made in regard to eggs; we did not paint any picture of the future of the poultry industry as being affected by that legislation. But we certainly did point out what the effect would be on the dairy industry, and the picture we painted at that time is quite visible to-day. So far as these other industries are concerned, they are vitally affected by the action of the government.
The minister referred to certain machinery set up in British Columbia to deal with this great problem of the fruit growers and he observed that no doubt, before next fall, many of us would be condemning the provincial government for its action in introducing that legislation. Let me direct his attention to the fact that the Premier of British

Dumping Duty-Mr. Barber
Columbia is to-day telling the people and the press of that part of the country that he is keeping the wires to Ottawa hot in protest against the action of this government in cancelling the order in council under discussion. More than that, according to a despatch in one of the coast papers, he made the statement that he had wired to his Minister of Lands, Mr. Pattullo, requesting him to join the large deputation that waited upon the government asking for a restoration of this legislation. We find, however, that Mr. Pattullo was not present in the delegation, although the people of British Columbia believe he was.
I am not going to discuss section 6 and section 47a; these two sections have been fully dealt with to-night. I should like to know, however, who suggested that the government should take this action, or for what reason they did so. There has been no demand from the consumers of the country. This order in council fixing the fair market values of the products affected has gone a great way towards stabilizing industries during the last two years. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other day intimated, I think, that no request had been filed with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr Euler) this season, or within the last few weeks, to have an order in council passed in regard to fixing fair values. I hold in my hand a telegram bearing date April 25 addressed to the hon. member for Yale, as follows:
Armstrong, B.C.
Have wired Minister of Customs to have fair price of asparagus dumped in from America set at twelve cents pound. Unless this is done it means ruination to B. C. Growers. We have half ton daily to ship from Armstrong. Please use influence to have this effected immediately.
Poole,
Fairfield Ranch.
This was a request from the growers in Armstrong, and they say that they have forwarded a demand to the Minister of National Revenue asking him to take the necessary steps to have an order in council passed fixing the price of this particular commodity. Then we have a request from the Canadian horticultural council, filed with the minister, bearing date March 12 and setting forth suggested prices and seasons. This was filed not only with the Minister of National Revenue but, as well, with the Minister of Agriculture. I will not read it, but I may point out that, in regard to strawberries, it was suggested that they be valued at ten cents per pound for duty purposes, from June 1 to July 31, while raspberries were fixed at fifteen cents, from June 15 to July 31. And so on down the
list. These are two requests that have been filed by the producers and the representatives with the department up to the present time.
I have had several protests from my district, copies of which, I believe, have been forwarded to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of National Revenue. I will not deal with them all; I intend to touch upon one or two only. I have one from Mission City dated April 13. This communication states that at a meeting held on the date mentioned, some 2,000 fruit and vegetable growers of British Columbia were represented, and that they earnestly endorsed the application already made by the associated growers requesting the immediate restoration of the order in council as provided in section 47a, now section 43 of the Customs Act. The present indications are, it is stated, that there will be a heavy dumping of American produce on the Canadian market, whereas the production in British Columbia will be in excess of the requirements of the prairie provinces. This is signed by the following: Fruit and Mercantile Exchange, Ltd.; Wilson Fruit and Produce Limited; Central Fruit Distributors Limited; Maple Ridge Co-operative Exchange; Japanese Consolidated Farmers Exchange; and Dewdney Rhubarb Growers Association.
I have another telegram from New Westminster embodying a resolution of a large mass meeting of poultry farmers, held there on April 23, protesting against the removal of the dumping duty; also a telegram from Port Haney, intimating a unanimous request on the part of the Maple Ridge Poultry Association that t'he federal member lodge a protest with the Minister of National Revenue, in the name of the association, urging that every effort be made to have the dumping duty restored, or a higher duty imposed on eggs coming into Canada from the United States.
A question has arisen, with some of our friends opposite, as to the principle of the matter; they are apparently opposed to antidumping legislation. The hon. member for Yale has already referred to the economic conference under the auspices of the League of Nations, and the Prime Minister has discussed the subject on more than one occasion in dealing with tariff matters. I wish to refer to the final report, at page 35 of which there is a statement regarding indirect means of protecting national trade. Section 2, which refers to dumping and anti-dumping, is as follows:
The conference recognizes that the question of dumping is of particular importance to those countries which have adopted a liberal tariff policy, and lays stress on the fact that, although

Dumping Duty-Mr. Esling

the consumer may secure, as a result of dumping, certain transitory advantages as regards price, there can be no doubt that dumping creates a state of insecurity in production and commerce, and can therefore exercise a harmful influence quite out of proportion to the temporary advantage resulting from cheap imports.
The same applies to dumping employed by powerful firms or commercial combines in one or more countries to destroy the similar industries of another country, and thus to enable them afterwards to raise the price on the market of that country.
It is certain that dumping is facilitated by the existence of high import duties in the countries practising it, and that it may lead to the introduction of high defensive duties in the importing country.
The conference considers that dumping must be reduced to a minimum, and that in order to attain this object, every possible measure should be taken to establish universally stable conditions of production and commerce and to reduce the excessive customs tariffs of exporting countries.
The conference recommends, however, that importing countries which find themselves compelled to take defensive measures against dumping should not resort to excessive, indirect or vexatious measures which would have a more far-reaching effect than is intended.
I think everyone will agree that the request we are making to-night on behalf of the producers of vegetables and fruits in this country is not unreasonable or excessive. The Minister of Finance has said a great deal about the tariff and has tried to drag the tariff across the path as a red herring. It is not a matter of tariff; it is a matter of fixing something upon which we can base a tariff. For instance, as it was explained the other day, a commodity may come to our borders which has no fixed value on which an ad valorem duty can apply. The idea of section 47a, and the reason for the power given the minister under that order in council, is to have a fair market value set upon that article on which a duty may be collected. This not only protects us from a cheap grade of fruits and vegetables but enables us to fix a basis upon which our duty can be collected, and on behalf of the producers of my district and those throughout the country I feel it my duty to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson).

If the producers of natural products in Canada are not to be encouraged at least to the extent of having their own home market, one naturally wonders why this government is spending about $3,000,000 a year to bring in immigrants to go on the land. In 1922 Hon. Mr. Fielding took exception to the provisions brought in by the Conservative government in 1921 to protect our markets against being flooded by fruit and farm products from the

United States. Mr. Fielding contended that those provisions were not workable, while the fruit growers and farmers took the stand that they were not only workable but were of great value in stopping the flooding of the Canadian market with fruits and vegetables from the United States at a time when the markets of that country were glutted. The then Minister of Customs, in keeping with Mr. Fielding's suggestion, brought in this amendment which has been known as section 47a and which is now section 43. When this session of parliament opened one of the first resolutions on the order paper was in the name of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), asking the government to rescind the order in council making it possible for the Minister of Customs to fix values for the purpose of customs duty. The hon. member suggested that it had been intimated from this side of the house that the withdrawal of that resolution was the result of threats, but I do not think the government has any fear of threats to-day, since they have a good majority in this house. However, the conclusion is general that the hon. member withdrew that resolution more particularfy for the purpose of saving this government considerable embarrassment, because we must not forget that this very order in council which has been rescinded was authorized by the section passed by the present government, with the approval of the Prime Minister and all his colleagues in the cabinet. I think this action was taken not only to save the government from embarrassment but to relieve hon. members from Quebec, many of whom would have had to vote against the government; and it also saved the Ontario Liberals some embarrassment. We must not overlook the Minister of Health (Mr. King), in whose political waverings I am always very much interested. When section 47a wias introduced, in defending it he said it was for protection against unfair and unreasonable competition, and that the amendment was only intended to overcome conditions which arose at certain times when there was an unfair competition under which the grower of natural products could not exist.
To be very brief, I simply wish to voice the protest of the farmers, fruit growers and poultry raisers of my district against. the cancellation of this order in council, and 1 hope the government may find some means of restoring it.

As the case has been so admirably presented to the house by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) and other speakers, I do not propose at this time to go into the question of the dumping

Dumping Duty-Mr. Fraser
clause at any great length. The fruit and vegetable industry of this country is sufficiently important that a person who represents a district which produces fruit should have something to say on this matter. The fruit and vegetable industry of Canada produced $48,500,000 last year, of which British Columbia produced $13,500,000, or about 28 per cent of the total fruit crop.
My district is inhabited to a very large extent by fruit growers, especially in the neighbourhood of Shusway lake, down to the end of the district near Yale. It contains a very valuable fruit-growing area, and, in deference to the wishes of the people who live in that section I wish to protest against the removal of this dumping duty. I should like to put on file some of the telegrams which I have received from that district. The first is from the Shusway Lake Co-operative Growers, and reads as follows:
Strongly endorse attitude of associated growers of British Columbia on question of dump duty. Rely on you to do utmost to get dumping protection as before.
They are simply asking for the dumping protection they had before.
Then I have another one from W. Crossley of Kamloops, as follows:
On behalf of Clearwater strawberry growers please protest vigorously against removal of dumping duties. Will mean ruin to us if duties removed as American late season rubbish spoils our market on prairie for high grade berries. Last year, although American growers got $5.50 per crate, when our crop ready they dumped several carloads on prairie market and forced price down to $2.75. This was to put us out of business. Urge application of dumping duty two weeks before our season opens and prevent unfair competition.
This shows the attitude of the strawberry growers of that district.
Then I have a letter from the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, protesting in the same way. Then I have another letter from the Salmon Arm Farmers' Exchange, protesting against the removal of the duty, and also a letter from the Associated Growers of British Columbia, Limited, representing the fruit growers in my section of British Columbia.
We find a peculiar situation in regard to some of the criticisms which have come from the other side of the house as to this duty. For instance, the member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) complains that the fruit growers of British Columbia co-operate in selling and distributing their fruit. I think they have a perfect right to co-operate in selling their fruit. You do not find British Columbia saying anything against the wheat pool on the prairies, and the fruit growers of that province
56103-191J
are just trying to do for themselves what the prairie men have been so successful in doing, and no more.
The pool is not enforced by fine and imprisonment.
There is no fine and imprisonment in connection with the British Columbia fruit growers.
There is.

Then we have the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) at which I am rather surprised. The Minister of Finance said that the fruit growers of British Columbia enjoy protection from the provincial government. I have the annual report of the Interior Tree, Fruit and Vegetable Committee of Direction, and I want to read a few paragraphs from that report for the benefit of the Minister of Finance. One paragraph, under the heading of "Setting of Prices", reads as follows:
The committee is charged with setting prices, "which shall be fair to the producer, retailer and consumer." This is not a particularly easy thing to do. In the last analysis it is the consuming public, who. at least, limit the prices obtainable. Again, the committee has felt that it may serve the industry better by helping obtain wide and sustained distribution at reasonable prices than by possibly restricting sales to merely a portion of a crop in an attempt to obtain spectacular prices.
That is, the object of the committee is to obtain reasonable prices in order to get wide distribution. Then it goes on to say:
It cannot always control the prices at which products must move. These are controlled by competitive or, sometimes, weather conditions, but it has certainly stabilized the industry and market to a noteworthy degree.
That is all the fruit growers of British Columbia are attempting to do, and I think it ill becomes either the Minister of Finance or the people of the prairie provinces to find fault with an organization which is only attempting to do what the wheat pool has done. No person in British Columbia has anything to say against the wheat pool; they all commend it and they are glad to see the people on the prairies enjoy the benefits from it, but we would like to have a little reciprocal treatment so far as our effort at co-operation is concerned.
I want to draw attention for a few moments to the attempt of the Prime Minister to make the delegation which waited on him a few days ago believe that the order in council was an attempt to fix duties or that the Customs officials were given the privilege and were using it to fix the tariff throughout the year. In his remarks to that delegation he went on to say that the government was
Technical Education

under the impression that the Department of National Revenue were given the power to fix the tariff. He said also that he was very much surprised to see they were exercising the right to fix the tariff to extend over the entire year, and he emphasized the fact that this order in council was giving them the power to fix the tariff throughout the year. At another place he said:
I wanted to bring out, and I think it has been brought out clearly-and if it has not been brought out clearly up to the present,
I would be glad to be interrupted by anyone who does not see it-that what the government is taking exception to is the giving to the Minister of Customs power to fix the duty on any classes of products that are named in these orders, notwithstanding the duties that are already fixed by parliament in the Customs Act.
At another place he goes on to say:
The government's attention has been drawn to the way in which this order in council was being applied by the officers of the Customs department. The order was never intended to give such power as that to the Minister of Customs, and the officials of his department, and if there is any doubt we had better have the orders cancelled altogether.
That is again pointing out the fact that they are fixing the tariff. The orders in council have been dealt with several times, but I want to point out that that is an entirely misleading statement for the Prime Minister of this country to make. There is no power to fix the tariff in any part of the orders in council. Power is given to fix the valuation for duty purposes, but not to fix the tariff. It is entirely a misrepresentation of the orders in council to say that that section fixes the tariff.
